newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Replica of 18th century ship revives Cook's legacy.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Replica of 18th century ship revives Cook's legacy.

text.p: He conquered scurvy, punctured the myth of a "Great Southern Continent", put New Zealand on the map, charted the southeastern coast of Australia and is recognised as the sailor's sailor.

An Australian organisation has paid Captain James Cook the posthumous compliment of building a replica of his first pioneering ship, the H.M. Bark Endeavour, in an effort to remind the 20th century of his legacy.

The H.M. Bark Endeavour Foundation, which launched the replica in Australia in 1993, hope the three-mast sailing ship will stimulate people to learn about Cook (1728-1779) and his world-shaping achievements.
Hundreds lined the banks of the Thames to welcome the ship as it meandered upriver in spring sunshine to moorings at the heart of London last month.

On its way it passed the Greenwich Observatory, through which the Meridian line runs from pole to pole, marking Greenwich Mean time. A lone cannon, mounted on the roof of a riverside pub next to the National Maritime Museum, fired a single welcoming shot.
Traffic was stopped from crossing Tower Bridge while it was raised to allow the Endeavour through.
The replica is a travelling museum, decked out with original artefacts designed to make the visitor feel as if Cook and his crew had stepped ashore only a moment before.
It was due to spend 17 days in London, where it will be open to the public, before setting off on a seven-month, 14-port British tour.
BRITISH TOUR

"Endeavour's forthcoming tour gives an opportunity for people in the UK to experience the conditions under which Cook and his men made their breakthrough voyages of discovery," said Richard Ormond, director of the National Maritime Museum, in a statement.

The replica Endeavour was launched in Fremantle, western Australia, 225 years after the original set sail from England. It has docked in South Africa, St Helena, the Ascension Islands, Tenerife and Madeira, and two years ago spent three months touring New Zealand. The Foundation said some 150,000 visitors had gone on board.
"We have already learnt a great deal about life at sea through the Endeavour, and will continue to do so," Ormond said. The ship is due to set sail for the United States in October.
AUTHENTIC REPLICA
The 109 feet and three inches (33.30 metres) long craft took six years to build, to exact specifications taken from plans kept in the vaults of the National Maritime Museum.
"The Foundation has constructed the most authentic replica ship in the world," Ormond boasted.
The original Endeavour was a classic coal carrier, solidly built, flat bottomed, and equipped with an ample hull for storage. It was a slow but sturdy vessel, capable of weathering the fiercest seas.

The replica has had to be fitted with radar equipment and a motor to meet modern seaworthiness regulations. Its hull is of Australian hardwood and masts of North American wood, both treated with preservatives to ensure a longer sea-life than the original elm, oak and spruce.
The replica is also better ventilated than the original, but the crew still sleep side-by-side in hammocks below deck. Cook had a crew of more than 90; the replica has 56.
Cook's original H.M. Bark Endeavour sailed from Portsmouth in southern England in August 1768 with a mission to chart the transit of Venus, the planet's rare passage across the face of the sun.
That done, he planned to search for the "Great Southern Continent", or "Terra Australis", which philosophers argued must exist to balance out the land masses of the Northern Hemisphere.
By the time the Endeavour had made it back to England in 1771, Cook had crossed the Atlantic, charted the movement of Venus, rounded Cape Horn and proved there was no continent south of Tahiti.

Cook was the first European to set foot on New Zealand, which he charted along with most of the southeast coast of Australia, and successfully navigated the dreaded Great Barrier Reef before stopping off in Indonesia on his way back to England.
His charts opened up the whole region for settlement and are so accurate that they can still be used today.
Perhaps Cook's greatest contribution to seafaring was the defeat of scurvy, a dietary disease caused by a lack of ascorbic acid that ravaged crews on long voyages during the 18th century.

He insisted on a diet that included cress, sauerkraut, and orange extract, and ensured the ship was well ventilated. The Endeavour was the first ship to undergo a long voyage without losing a man to scurvy.
Cook was also the first to determine longitude accurately at sea using nautical tables and lunar sights.
His voyages left a trail of place names including the Cook Islands and Australia's Botany Bay, so named simply because the Endeavour had so many botanists on board.
